abstract.t: A profile of RFC 7748 for nish/crypto/x25519: the X25519 function, its scalar and u-coordinate encodings, the iterated test vectors and the Diffie-Hellman exchange on Curve25519. Every requirement quotes RFC 7748, the main source; every binding sentence of RFC 7748 (MUST, MUST NOT, SHALL, SHALL NOT, REQUIRED) is tested or excluded here. X448 is not implemented and not profiled.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

nish/crypto/x25519 exports x25519, the function of RFC 7748 Section 5, and x25519Base, the same function on the base point u = 9. The scalar and the shared secret are Secret values; the properties see them as bytes. Both functions return null unless every argument is 32 bytes, and an all-zero result (Section 6.1) is returned, not refused, so no clause here tests a refusal of it.

The iterated vectors of Section 5.2 are vector rows, each with an Iterate: paragraph after the table. The 1,000,000-iteration one is marked slow, so the emitted test runs it only with --slow.

The Section 6.1 test vector is the property P-DH-VECTOR rather than vector rows: the section prints its values under names such as "Alice's private key, a", which a vector label cannot spell (vector 0.3.1 refuses such a row's Call and Expected as "not a literal"), and the profile refuses an unlabelled value printed under a name. Its bytes are transcribed from the RFC, so fidelity does not check them. Its zero argument takes the single value 0: a property needs a forall argument, and this one has no input to vary.

section.name: Interface
The X25519 Function

blockquote.t: The functions take a scalar and a u-coordinate as inputs and produce a u-coordinate as output.
Although the functions work internally with integers, the inputs and outputs are 32-byte strings (for X25519) or 56-byte strings (for X448) and this specification defines their encoding.
When receiving such an array, implementations of X25519 (but not X448) MUST mask the most significant bit in the final byte.
Implementations MUST accept non-canonical values and process them as if they had been reduced modulo the field prime.

For X25519, in order to decode 32 random bytes as an integer scalar, set the three least significant bits of the first byte and the most significant bit of the last to zero, set the second most significant bit of the last byte to 1 and, finally, decode as little-endian.
Finally, encode the resulting value as 32 or 56 bytes in little- endian order.
For X25519, the unused, most significant bit MUST be zero.
The cswap function SHOULD be implemented in constant time (i.e., independent of the swap argument).

section.t: Untested: timing is not observable by a functional test; nish checks it on the emitted machine code (tests/cases/ct_asm_x25519.ts, tests/ct-timing.js, docs/security/ct-verification.md, docs/security/crypto-ecc.md)

blockquote.t: For each iteration, set k to be the result of calling the function and u to be the old value of k.

Alice generates 32 random bytes in a[0] to a[31] and transmits K_A = X25519(a, 9) to Bob, where 9 is the u-coordinate of the base point and is encoded as a byte with value 9, followed by 31 zero bytes.
Both now share K = X25519(a, X25519(b, 9)) = X25519(b, X25519(a, 9)) as a shared secret.

section.name: Deterministic Generation

blockquote.t: The trace of Frobenius MUST NOT be in {0, 1} in order to rule out the attacks described in [smart], [satoh], and [semaev], as in [brainpool] and [safecurves].

abstract.t: This memo specifies two elliptic curves over prime fields that offer a high level of practical security in cryptographic applications, including Transport Layer Security (TLS). These curves are intended to operate at the ~128-bit and ~224-bit security level, respectively, and are generated deterministically based on a list of required properties.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
